scribe_response.text: What do you remember about your school days? My school days began at six, in a one-story school near the Iloilo market. It had a red tin roof, a flagpole, and a yard that turned to soup in rain. I walked there barefoot with my two sisters, carrying books tied with rubber strap. My um mother ironed my white blouse every Sunday night with an iron full of hot coals. She polished my one pair of black shoes, and I carried them in a cloth bag. At the gate I put them on, because a, a student should look um like a student. Our first teacher was Missus Dayrit, a round woman with a voice like a church bell. She had a long wooden pointer that she used only on the blackboard and the occasional fly. We sat three to a desk, on benches worn smooth by generations. I loved the smell of chalk dust and the squeak of the wiped board. We learned to write in copybooks with blue lines and a rooster on the cover. My handwriting was neat, and um Missus Dayrit pinned my page on the wall. I was so proud that I tripped over a goat on the way home. What happened next? Every morning we stood in rows, sang the anthem, and stretched our arms wide. Then we recited the multiplication tables, and the sound rolled across the yard like waves. Arithmetic was my best subject, but stories were what I loved most. Missus Dayrit also taught us to sing, mostly songs about rain and rice. The school library was one shelf in a cupboard that smelled of mildew. I read um every book on it twice, even a thick one about the stars. At um lunchtime we sat under the acacia tree and opened our tin boxes of rice. A boy named Jun always, Jun always traded his dried fish for my sweet rice cake. On rainy days the teacher let us tell stories, and those were my favorite afternoons. I discovered then that people listened to me if I used my hands. Of course I also got into trouble, as every child does. Once I drew the principal with a fish for a nose on my notebook. My friend Tess laughed so um hard that she fell off the bench. We were both sent to stand in the corner. Can you tell me more about that? Standing there, I felt terrible, but I also felt a small thrill of rebellion. My mother, My mother heard about it that evening and gave me a look worse than any scolding. Then she laughed, because she never could stay angry with me for long. At the school fiesta we staged a play about a girl who saved her village. I was the girl, with a crown of banana leaves and a cape made from a um curtain. I forgot my lines in the middle, so I made up new ones, and the audience clapped. That was the day I decided I uh wanted um to stand in front of a room and talk. The war had left, left some of um our books torn, and the walls were patched with plywood. We had little, but our teachers treated every child as a future doctor. They gave us the gift of believing we could be somebody, and never charged a peso. When I became a teacher myself, I tried to um give that same gift to every child. Even now, when I smell chalk, I am six years old again with tight braids. In the dry months we played tag until the dust turned our uniforms brown. I would go back for one more morning with the anthem and the tables.
